sourceText: Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the LEM-SOLARIS sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. The ocean produces forms connected to the children's memories, but no one knows whether they are communication, experiment, or reflex. The memorial bore the name of Stanisław Lem — Solaris precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Contact was the only domain in which success could mean leaving without an answer. Aster, built to reduce uncertainty, found that criterion almost painful. Tern had specialized in things that did not answer. In a family built for exploration, he had become the custodian of the right to silence. At the center of the conflict was Yen, an administrator chosen precisely because they were not a specialist in the phenomenon that had reorganized the world. ‘The specialists tell me what can be done,’ they said. ‘I have to answer who it may be done to.’ Kesh kept the distinction in his notes. 271 The problem closed quickly around them: Aster refuses aggressive scanning, and Tern accuses her of turning present caution into retroactive guilt. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Lp — Living Planet: the biosphere or planet functions as an agent; Nc — Impossible Contact: the parties do not share sufficient categories. Course references included Stanisław Lem — Solaris. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Tern broke the first consensus. ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ Orin answered without raising their voice: ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. 272 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS Orin asked for a simulation of the option the group had just rejected. Aster gave him only the non-conscious model. He did not want to manufacture victims in order to validate his guilt; he wanted a map of absent costs. The distinction had become one of their working rules. The night did not end in victory. The ocean reproduces the outside signal with a single mathematical relation altered — enough to encode coordinates. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. The outside residue had become stable enough that Tern could predict where it would not appear: in sectors fully indexed by Aster. He began to believe that the message carried no content at all, but instead demonstrated a boundary — a region in which their instruments received no echo from their own creator. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the INVERSION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — reverses an order, dependence, direction, or relation taken as natural — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has 273 to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. In the hall between sectors, Aster’s Hunger returned. None of the children tried to soothe it. They had begun to believe that some pains should not immediately be turned into demands upon the people nearby. 274 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
